Arc length $l=r\theta$:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{5\pi}{2} &= r\theta \\ r &= \dfrac{5\pi}{2\theta} \quad (1) \end{aligned}$$

Sector area $A=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta$:

$$\dfrac{15\pi}{4}=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta \quad (2)$$

Substitute (1) into (2):

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{15\pi}{4} &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{2\theta}\right)^2\theta \\ \dfrac{15\pi}{4} &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{25\pi^2}{4\theta} \\ 30 &= \dfrac{25\pi}{\theta} \\ \theta &= \dfrac{25\pi}{30} \\ &= \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \end{aligned}$$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 3: Correct answer; 2: Solves the simultaneous equations, or equivalent merit; 1: Uses $l=r\theta$ to find $r=\dfrac{5\pi}{2\theta}$, or equivalent merit

Quotient rule with $u=(x-1)^{\frac{1}{2}}$, $u'=\dfrac{1}{2}(x-1)^{-\frac{1}{2}}$, $v=x^2$, $v'=2x$:

When $x=2$:

$$\begin{aligned} y' &= \dfrac{\frac{1}{2}(2)^2(2-1)^{-\frac{1}{2}}-2(2)(2-1)^{\frac{1}{2}}}{2^4} \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{8} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ m_T=-\dfrac{1}{8}$$

$$\begin{aligned} FV &= FV_{\text{lump}}+FV_{\text{instal}} \\ &= P(1+r)^n+M\times\text{factor} \\ &= 1233.56(1+0.5\%)^{12}+200\times 12.3356 \\ &= 3776.763\ldots \\ &\approx 3776.76 \end{aligned}$$

$\therefore$ Hannah has \$3776.76.

The fund runs out when $A_n=0$:

$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= 3776.76(1.005)^n-80400(1.005)^n+80400 \\ &= -76623.24(1.005)^n+80400 \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} 76623.24(1.005)^n &= 80400 \\ (1.005)^n &= 1.049\ldots \\ n\ln 1.005 &= \ln 1.049\ldots \\ n &= 9.64\ldots \end{aligned}$$

$\therefore$ Hannah can make 9 withdrawals.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 2: Correct answer, including rounding down; 1: Sets $A_n=0$ and simplifies to $-76623.24(1.005)^n+80400=0$, or equivalent merit

The total probability is 1:

$$\begin{aligned} 1 &= \int_0^4 ke^x\,dx+\int_4^{10} ke\,dx \\ &= \Big[ke^x\Big]_0^4+\Big[kex\Big]_4^{10} \\ &= ke^4-ke^0+10ke-4ke \\ &= ke^4-k+6ke \\ &= k(e^4+6e-1) \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{1}{e^4+6e-1}$$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 2: Correct answer; 1: Correct integration of both pieces, or equivalent merit

$$\begin{aligned} 0.5 &= \int_0^x \dfrac{1}{e^4+6e-1}e^t\,dt \\ &= \dfrac{1}{e^4+6e-1}\Big[e^t\Big]_0^x \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} 34.9\ldots &= e^x-e^0 \\ &= e^x-1 \\ e^x &= 35.9\ldots \\ x &= \ln 35.9\ldots \\ &= 3.582\ldots \text{ minutes} \\ &\approx 3 \text{ min } 35 \text{ s} \end{aligned}$$

The parabola is above $y=-\sqrt{2x+16}$ for $0\le x\le 10$:

$$\begin{aligned} A &= \int_0^{10}\left(-\dfrac{x^2}{25}+\dfrac{x}{5}-4-\left(-(2x+16)^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)\right)dx \\ &= \int_0^{10}\left(-\dfrac{x^2}{25}+\dfrac{x}{5}-4\right)dx+\dfrac{1}{2}\int_0^{10}2(2x+16)^{\frac{1}{2}}\,dx \\ &= \left[-\dfrac{x^3}{75}+\dfrac{x^2}{10}-4x\right]_0^{10}+\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{2(2x+16)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\right]_0^{10} \\ &= \left(-\dfrac{10^3}{75}+\dfrac{10^2}{10}-4(10)-0\right)+\left(\dfrac{(2(10)+16)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}-\dfrac{(2(0)+16)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\right) \\ &= -\dfrac{130}{3}+\dfrac{152}{3} \\ &= \dfrac{22}{3}\text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 4: Correct answer; 3: Correct substitution of the limits, or equivalent merit; 2: Correct primitives, or equivalent merit; 1: Correct integral expression for the area, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Product rule with $u=10e^{-x}$, $u'=-10e^{-x}$, $v=1-x$, $v'=-1$:

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= vu'+uv' \\ &= -10e^{-x}(1-x)-10e^{-x} \\ &= -10e^{-x}(1-x+1) \\ &= -10e^{-x}(2-x) \end{aligned}$$

Stationary points when $f'(x)=0$: $-10e^{-x}=0$ has no solutions, so $2-x=0$, $x=2$.

Product rule with $u=-10e^{-x}$, $u'=10e^{-x}$, $v=2-x$, $v'=-1$:

$$\begin{aligned} f''(x) &= vu'+uv' \\ &= 10e^{-x}(2-x)+10e^{-x} \\ &= 10e^{-x}(3-x) \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} f''(2) &= 10e^{-2}(3-2) \\ &= 1.3\ldots>0 \end{aligned}$$

so a local minimum.

$$\begin{aligned} f(2) &= 10e^{-2}(1-2) \\ &= -10e^{-2} \end{aligned}$$

$\therefore$ $(2,-10e^{-2})$ is a local minimum.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 3: Correct answer; 2: Finds $x=2$ and shows it is a local minimum, or equivalent merit; 1: Correct $f'(x)$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{Charlie wins}) &= P(\bar{M}C)+P(\bar{M}\bar{C}\bar{M}C)+P(\bar{M}\bar{C}\bar{M}\bar{C}\bar{M}C)+\cdots \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{3}+\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{2}{3}\times\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{3}+\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{2}{3}\times\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{2}{3}\times\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{3}+\cdots \end{aligned}$$

This is an infinite geometric series with $a=\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{3}=\dfrac{1}{6}$ and $r=\dfrac{2}{3}\times\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{1}{3}$:

$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= \dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{6}\div\left(1-\dfrac{1}{3}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{4} \end{aligned}$$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 2: Correct answer; 1: Identifies the infinite geometric series with $a=\dfrac{1}{6}$ and $r=\dfrac{1}{3}$, or equivalent merit
